title: The Journey to the Great Oz, part 1
attribution: From The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum (1900), via Project Gutenberg, in reading order.
body: They were obliged to camp out that night under a large tree in the forest, for there were no houses near. The tree made a good, thick covering to protect them from the dew, and the Tin Woodman chopped a great pile of wood with his axe and Dorothy built a splendid fire that warmed her and made her feel less lonely. She and Toto ate the last of their bread, and now she did not know what they would do for breakfast.

“If you wish,” said the Lion, “I will go into the forest and kill a deer for you. You can roast it by the fire, since your tastes are so peculiar that you prefer cooked food, and then you will have a very good breakfast.”
“Don’t! Please don’t,” begged the Tin Woodman. “I should certainly weep if you killed a poor deer, and then my jaws would rust again.”

But the Lion went away into the forest and found his own supper, and no one ever knew what it was, for he didn’t mention it. And the Scarecrow found a tree full of nuts and filled Dorothy’s basket with them, so that she would not be hungry for a long time. She thought this was very kind and thoughtful of the Scarecrow, but she laughed heartily at the awkward way in which the poor creature picked up the nuts. His padded hands were so clumsy and the nuts were so small that he dropped almost as many as he put in the basket. But the Scarecrow did not mind how long it took him to fill the basket, for it enabled him to keep away from the fire, as he feared a spark might get into his straw and burn him up. So he kept a good distance away from the flames, and only came near to cover Dorothy with dry leaves when she lay down to sleep. These kept her very snug and warm, and she slept soundly until morning.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why did the party camp under a tree?
options: There were no houses near
The Lion refused to walk further
A storm was coming on quickly
The road had given out entirely

questions.prompt: Per the passage, who chopped the pile of wood for the fire?
options: The Tin Woodman
The Cowardly Lion
Dorothy and Toto
The Scarecrow

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Scarecrow fill Dorothy's basket with?
options: Nuts
Ripe fruit
Dry leaves
Bread from the cottage

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Lion offer to do?
options: Go into the forest and kill a deer
Carry Dorothy on his back all night
Keep watch beside the fire till dawn
Frighten away the other beasts

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Scarecrow cover Dorothy with?
options: Dry leaves
His own blue coat
A pile of straw
The white cloth

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Tin Woodman beg the Lion not to hunt?
options: He would weep over the deer and rust his jaws
He wanted the party to reach the city hungry
He thought the Lion would be caught by the Kalidahs
He had already found food for Dorothy himself

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did the Scarecrow not mind how long the nuts took?
options: It kept him at a safe distance from the fire
He enjoyed being useful to Dorothy at last
He had nothing else to do until morning
He was hoping to find brains among the nuts

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why did Dorothy laugh at the Scarecrow gathering nuts?
options: His padded hands dropped nearly as many as he gathered
He kept mistaking stones for nuts in the dark
He insisted on carrying the basket on his head
He talked the whole time instead of working

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does the Lion mean by calling Dorothy's tastes peculiar?
options: Odd, because she prefers her food cooked
Expensive, because she will only eat deer
Delicate, because she eats so very little
Strict, because she refuses to eat meat

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the passage?
options: A night in the open where each companion provides what he can
A night in which the party runs out of food entirely
A quarrel about whether animals should be killed for food
A long walk that ends without anywhere to shelter

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did Dorothy and Toto eat that night?
options: The last of their bread
Nuts from the Scarecrow's tree
Roast deer from the Lion's hunt
Fruit found beside the road

questions.prompt: Per the passage, what did the Lion do about his own supper?
options: Found it in the forest and never mentioned it
Went without any supper at all that night
Shared the nuts the Scarecrow had gathered
Killed a deer and roasted it on the fire

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the thick tree protect them from?
options: The dew
The wind
The rain
The Kalidahs

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what did the fire do for Dorothy besides warm her?
options: It made her feel less lonely
It kept the wild beasts away
It showed the road ahead
It dried out her wet clothes

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what is the Scarecrow afraid might happen near the flames?
options: A spark might catch his straw and burn him up
The heat might melt the paint from his face
The smoke might blind his painted eyes
His clothes might be scorched beyond mending

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the leaves kept Dorothy snug?
options: Warm and comfortable
Hidden from view
Dry but uncomfortable
Still and unable to move

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarises the passage?
options: Three companions who need nothing themselves look after the one who does
A hunting trip that leaves the party with food for many days
An argument about cooked food that divides the travellers
A sleepless night spent guarding the camp against beasts
